tip: 'À peine fut-il sorti que' = 'barely had he left when.' Fronting 'à peine' flips subject and verb ('fut-il'), just like the English inversion.
'Le bât blesse' = 'the packsaddle hurts'. Where the problem lies.
'Ce en quoi je crois' = 'what I believe in': the verb is 'croire en' (believe in), so its 'en' sits before 'quoi' instead of dangling at the end.
Classic fairy tale ending. 'Vécurent' is the literary past (passé simple) of 'vivre' (to live).
'Eut prononcé' is the literary past-in-the-past of 'prononcer' (to utter), used after 'aussitôt que' / 'dès que' in written narration.
'Rares sont les occasions' fronts the adjective for emphasis, flipping verb and subject – literally 'rare are the chances.'
'Dont' replaces 'de': 'la manière dont il a réagi' = 'the way in which he reacted' ('réagir de cette manière').
'Eut pleuré' is the literary past-in-the-past, standing in for 'avait pleuré' after 'après que'. You'll meet it only in written narration.
Word for word this idiom is 'the butter and the money from the butter' – 'le beurre et l'argent du beurre'. French says you can't keep the butter and pocket what you sold it for too.
'Ne sauraient' looks like 'would know', but 'savoir' in the conditional means 'cannot' – a soft, formal impossibility: 'ne sauraient être occultés' = 'cannot be concealed'.
French says an event 'has place' rather than 'takes place': 'avoir lieu'. 'La cérémonie a eu lieu' = 'the ceremony took place' – no word for 'take' anywhere in it.
French drops the 'his' here: it's 'faire fortune', not 'faire sa fortune'. 'Il fit fortune' = 'he made his fortune' – the possessive lives only in the English.
'Force est de constater' = 'one can only note': a formal set phrase, literally 'force is to note', used to concede an unavoidable fact.
'Cherchez la femme' – 'look for the woman' – comes from Dumas: the notion that a woman is behind whatever tangle you're puzzling over.
'Mieux vaut' = 'it is better': a set phrase that drops the usual 'il' of 'il vaut mieux'.
Literally 'those who resemble each other gather together' – and 'ressemble' / 'assemble' rhyme, which is why the proverb lodges in your head.
'Demeure entière' is literally 'remains whole' – not one part of the question has been answered. Formal style.
'Habit' here is a false friend: French 'habit' means a garment – the monk's robe – not a routine. Literally 'the robe doesn't make the monk.'
'Nous nous garderons de' is literally 'we'll guard ourselves from' – the reflexive turns 'guard' into 'refrain from.' Formal caution.
'Sans appel' = unequivocal/beyond dispute. Literally 'without appeal' (legal metaphor).
'Force m'est de' means 'I'm compelled to' – literally 'force is upon me to': 'm'est' = 'is to me', marking who has no choice. Very formal.
That 'serait' (would be), not 'est' (is), softens the claim – French academic writing hedges with the conditional to sound less absolute.
'Nous nous attacherons à' is literally 'we'll attach ourselves to' demonstrating – the reflexive image means to commit to the task. Formal.
'Pallier' takes a direct object: 'pallier les insuffisances', never 'pallier à' – unlike 'remédier à'. Even native speakers slip on this one.
'Qui vivra verra' puts both verbs in the future: literally 'who will live will see'.
Literally 'To want is to be able.' French uses a bare infinitive as the subject – 'vouloir' means 'wanting' – and 'c'est' bridges it to the second infinitive 'pouvoir.'
'Ont toujours tort' – 'avoir tort' is literally 'to have wrong.' French uses 'have', not 'be', for being at fault, and the absent always cop the blame.
'Petit à petit' = 'little by little.' French doubles a word around 'à' for a step-by-step feel: 'peu à peu', 'côte à côte', 'goutte à goutte'.
'Loin des yeux, loin du cœur' is literally 'far from the eyes, far from the heart' – where English says 'out of sight, out of mind'.
'Quoi qu'il en soit' = 'be that as it may'. A fixed expression: 'quoi que' + subjunctive ('soit'). Very formal.
